stem: 'US hegemony' in world politics refers to the situation after the Cold War in which __________.
options: The United States became the sole superpower, dominant in military, economic, and cultural terms, with no rival able to balance it
The USSR dominated the world
China ruled the world
There were two equal superpowers
solution: 'US hegemony' refers to the post-Cold-War situation in which the UNITED STATES became the SOLE superpower and the DOMINANT power in world politics — pre-eminent in MILITARY, ECONOMIC, and CULTURAL/technological terms — with NO rival power or bloc able to effectively balance or check it. This dominance defined the 'unipolar' world that followed the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991. So US hegemony means US dominance as the sole superpower. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The chapter identifies that US hegemony operates in at least three senses/domains. These are hegemony as __________.
options: Hard power (military dominance), structural power (shaping the global economy/systems), and soft power (cultural/ideological influence)
Only military power
Only economic aid
Only cultural exports
solution: The chapter analyses US hegemony in three senses/domains: (1) hegemony as HARD POWER — overwhelming MILITARY dominance (unmatched armed forces, technology, and global reach); (2) hegemony as STRUCTURAL power — the US role in shaping the underlying STRUCTURES of the global economy and international system (e.g., the dominance of the dollar, and institutions and 'public goods' like sea lanes and the internet's origins); and (3) hegemony as SOFT POWER — the CULTURAL and IDEOLOGICAL INFLUENCE and appeal of the American way of life, values, and consumer culture. So US hegemony operates as hard, structural, and soft power. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 9/11 attacks (11 September 2001), which greatly influenced US foreign policy, were __________.
options: Coordinated terrorist attacks on the USA (including on the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon)
A war between the USA and USSR
A natural disaster
A US attack on another country
solution: The 9/11 attacks of 11 September 2001 were a series of coordinated TERRORIST attacks on the UNITED STATES, carried out by the Al-Qaeda network. Hijacked passenger planes were flown into the twin towers of the WORLD TRADE CENTER in New York (destroying them) and into the PENTAGON (the US defence headquarters), with another crashing in Pennsylvania; thousands were killed. These attacks profoundly shocked the USA and shaped its subsequent foreign policy — notably the 'War on Terror'. So 9/11 was a major terrorist attack on the USA. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: In response to the 9/11 attacks, the USA launched a global campaign known as the __________.
options: 'War on Terror'
'Marshall Plan'
'New Deal'
'Cold War'
solution: In response to the 9/11 attacks, the USA (under President George W. Bush) launched a global campaign known as the 'WAR ON TERROR' (the war against terrorism). This involved military operations (such as the invasion of Afghanistan to destroy Al-Qaeda and the Taliban regime that harboured it, and later the invasion of Iraq), as well as a wide range of security, intelligence, financial, and diplomatic measures against terrorist networks and states accused of supporting them. So the campaign was the 'War on Terror'. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: As part of the 'War on Terror', the USA led a military invasion of __________ in 2001 to overthrow the Taliban regime and target Al-Qaeda.
options: Afghanistan
Iraq
Iran
Cuba
solution: As the first major military campaign of the 'War on Terror', the USA led an invasion of AFGHANISTAN in 2001 (Operation Enduring Freedom). The aim was to destroy the AL-QAEDA network (blamed for 9/11) and to overthrow the TALIBAN regime, which had harboured Al-Qaeda and its leader Osama bin Laden. The Taliban government was quickly toppled, though the conflict in Afghanistan continued for many years. So the 2001 invasion was of Afghanistan. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: In 2003, the USA led another controversial invasion, this time of __________, on the (later discredited) grounds that it possessed 'weapons of mass destruction'.
options: Iraq
Afghanistan
Libya
Syria
solution: In 2003, the USA (with some allies, notably Britain — the 'coalition of the willing') led an invasion of IRAQ, called 'Operation Iraqi Freedom'. The main stated justifications were that Iraq (under Saddam Hussein) possessed 'WEAPONS of MASS DESTRUCTION' (WMDs) and had links to terrorism — claims that were LATER DISCREDITED (no WMDs were found). The invasion, carried out without clear UN authorisation and against much international opposition, toppled Saddam Hussein but led to prolonged instability and became a symbol of the controversial exercise of US power. So the 2003 invasion was of Iraq. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The US invasion of Iraq (2003) is often cited as an example of the exercise of US hegemony because it __________.
options: Was undertaken largely unilaterally (without clear UN Security Council authorisation), showing the USA's willingness and ability to act militarily against the wishes of much of the world
Was fully authorised by the whole world
Was a defensive war on US soil
Was led by the United Nations
solution: The US invasion of Iraq (2003) is often cited as a stark example of US hegemony because it was undertaken largely UNILATERALLY — WITHOUT clear authorisation from the UN Security Council, and against strong OPPOSITION from much of the international community (including major powers and global public opinion). It thus demonstrated the USA's WILLINGNESS and ABILITY to use its overwhelming military power to act as it chose, even against the wishes of most of the world and outside the framework of international institutions. This unchecked exercise of power is a hallmark of hegemony. So the Iraq invasion showed the USA acting unilaterally against world opinion. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Hegemony as hard power' refers primarily to the USA's __________.
options: Overwhelming and unmatched military capability (in spending, technology, and global reach)
Popular films and music
Control of the UN budget
Large population
solution: 'Hegemony as HARD POWER' refers primarily to the USA's overwhelming and UNMATCHED MILITARY capability. The USA spends more on defence than the next several countries combined, possesses the most advanced military TECHNOLOGY, and has unrivalled GLOBAL REACH (bases, navies, and forces able to project power anywhere in the world). This vast, coercive military superiority — the ability to use or threaten force on a global scale — is the 'hard power' dimension of US dominance. So hegemony as hard power means the USA's overwhelming military capability. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Hegemony as structural power' refers to the USA's role in __________.
options: Shaping and underpinning the structures of the global economy and system (e.g., the dominance of the US dollar, and providing global 'public goods' like open sea lanes)
Winning wars only
Making Hollywood films
Controlling the weather
solution: 'Hegemony as STRUCTURAL power' refers to the USA's role in SHAPING and underpinning the very STRUCTURES and rules of the GLOBAL ECONOMY and international system. Examples include: the dominance of the US DOLLAR as the world's main reserve and trading currency; the influence of the USA over global economic institutions and norms; and the provision of certain global 'PUBLIC GOODS' — such as keeping open the sea lanes of communication (SLOCs) for trade, and even the origins of the internet — on which the functioning of the global system depends. This underlying, system-shaping power is 'structural' hegemony. So it refers to the USA shaping the structures of the global economy/system. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Hegemony as soft power' refers to the USA's __________.
options: Cultural and ideological influence and appeal — its way of life, values, consumer culture, education, and entertainment, which attract and influence people worldwide
Nuclear weapons
Trade tariffs
Army bases
solution: 'Hegemony as SOFT POWER' refers to the USA's CULTURAL and IDEOLOGICAL INFLUENCE and APPEAL — its capacity to attract, persuade, and shape preferences (rather than coerce). This includes the global reach and appeal of the American WAY of LIFE, its VALUES (liberty, democracy, individualism), its CONSUMER culture and brands, its ENTERTAINMENT (Hollywood, music), and its universities and EDUCATION, which draw people worldwide and spread American norms and aspirations. Soft power is the ability to get others to want what you want. So hegemony as soft power means the USA's cultural/ideological attractiveness. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The chapter discusses how US hegemony can be constrained or checked. One internal constraint on US power is __________.
options: The USA's own institutional structure — the division/separation of powers among the branches of government (which can limit executive action)
The lack of any army
Complete absence of an economy
The rule of a foreign power over the USA
solution: The chapter notes that US hegemony is not entirely unlimited; it faces certain CONSTRAINTS. One INTERNAL constraint is the USA's own INSTITUTIONAL STRUCTURE — particularly the CONSTITUTIONAL division/SEPARATION of POWERS among the branches of government (the executive/President, the legislature/Congress, and the judiciary). This system of checks and balances means that the President's ability to exercise power (e.g., to wage war or set policy) can be LIMITED or checked by Congress and the courts, preventing wholly unchecked executive action. So one internal constraint is the US separation of powers. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Another constraint on American hegemony identified in the chapter is __________.
options: The open nature of American society and its free press/public opinion, which can question and check government actions
The lack of any media in the USA
A ban on public debate
The absence of citizens
solution: Another constraint on American power identified in the chapter is the OPEN, democratic nature of AMERICAN SOCIETY itself — particularly its FREE PRESS/media and vigorous PUBLIC OPINION and civil society. In an open society, the government's actions (including military interventions and foreign policy) can be QUESTIONED, scrutinised, criticised, and CHECKED by the media, public debate, and citizens, which can constrain what the government is able to do (e.g., sustained public opposition to unpopular wars). So the open nature of US society and its free press act as a constraint. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A third possible check on US hegemony discussed is __________.
options: The role of international organisations (like the UN) and of other states/coalitions (e.g., NATO allies, or a potential balance of power) that can, to some extent, limit or influence US actions
Nothing can ever check the USA
The weather
A single individual acting alone
solution: A third possible check on US hegemony discussed in the chapter is the role of INTERNATIONAL ORGANISATIONS (like the UNITED NATIONS) and of OTHER STATES and coalitions. Although the USA is dominant, international bodies and other powers can, to SOME extent, LIMIT, influence, or complicate US actions — for example, the UN and world opinion can withhold legitimacy from unilateral actions; ALLIANCE partners (like NATO allies) have their own views; and a potential coming together of other major powers (a BALANCE of power) could constrain the USA. (These checks are limited but real.) So a third check is international organisations and other states/coalitions. So option 1 is correct.

stem: One strategy suggested for how weaker states or a country like India might deal with US hegemony is 'bandwagoning', which means __________.
options: Working WITH the hegemon (extracting benefits by cooperating with and taking advantage of the opportunities the hegemonic system offers) rather than opposing it
Directly attacking the hegemon
Completely ignoring the hegemon
Forming a military alliance against all other countries
solution: 'BANDWAGONING' is one strategy for dealing with a hegemon: instead of resisting or balancing against it, a state chooses to WORK WITH the hegemon — extracting BENEFITS and OPPORTUNITIES from cooperation and from operating within the hegemonic system (e.g., gaining from trade, investment, technology, and good relations with the dominant power). Rather than opposing the hegemon (which may be costly or futile), the state 'hops on the bandwagon' to advance its own interests. (This is contrasted with strategies like 'balancing' against, or 'hiding'/keeping a low profile from, the hegemon.) So bandwagoning means working with the hegemon to gain benefits. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Another strategy, favoured by some who resist hegemony, is to strengthen __________ as a way of gradually creating a more balanced world.
options: International cooperation, coalitions of states, and institutions (and the rise of alternative power centres) to collectively balance or moderate the hegemon's power
The hegemon's military further
Isolation from all other countries
One's own dictatorship
solution: Another strategy for those who wish to RESIST or moderate hegemony is to strengthen INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION, COALITIONS of states, and INSTITUTIONS — and to encourage the rise of ALTERNATIVE POWER CENTRES — so as to COLLECTIVELY BALANCE, check, or moderate the hegemon's power over time. Since no single state can balance the hegemon alone, weaker states may band together (through alliances, regional blocs, and multilateral institutions) to create a more balanced, MULTIPOLAR world in which the hegemon's dominance is constrained. So this strategy involves building cooperation, coalitions, and alternative power centres to balance the hegemon. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India's relationship with the USA in the era of US hegemony has been characterised by __________.
options: Growing engagement and cooperation (in trade, technology, defence, and diplomacy), while India also seeks to maintain its strategic autonomy and independent foreign policy
Complete hostility and no contact
India becoming a US colony
India joining a military bloc against the USA
solution: In the era of US hegemony (post-Cold War), India's relationship with the USA has been characterised by GROWING ENGAGEMENT and COOPERATION — in areas such as TRADE and investment, TECHNOLOGY (including information technology and the large Indian diaspora/professionals in the USA), DEFENCE and strategic ties, and DIPLOMACY (e.g., the India–US civil nuclear deal). At the same time, India continues to value and assert its STRATEGIC AUTONOMY and INDEPENDENT foreign policy — engaging with the USA on its own terms while also maintaining relations with other powers (like Russia and its neighbours) and not simply aligning itself as a subordinate. So India's approach combines engagement/cooperation with the USA and preserving its strategic autonomy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The debate within India on how to relate to US hegemony includes different views. Which of the following is one such view?
options: Some argue India should stay away from the USA and focus on building coalitions of developing/like-minded countries to counter US dominance; others argue India should take advantage of close US ties to advance its own growth and interests
Everyone in India agrees India should oppose the USA in war
India should give up its sovereignty to the USA
There is no debate; all views are identical
solution: There are DIFFERENT VIEWS within India on how to relate to US hegemony. One view holds that India should keep its DISTANCE from the USA and instead focus on building COALITIONS of developing and like-minded countries (and strengthening bodies like NAM and regional groupings) to COUNTER and balance US dominance and promote a more equitable world order. Another view holds that India should TAKE ADVANTAGE of close ties with the USA — leveraging trade, investment, technology, and strategic cooperation — to advance its OWN economic GROWTH, security, and national INTERESTS. (Yet others advocate a pragmatic mix.) So the debate spans these differing strategies. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The chapter suggests that US hegemony, though dominant, may not be permanent because __________.
options: History shows hegemonies eventually decline, and the rise of new powers (like China, the EU, India), economic challenges, overextension, and shifting balances may erode US dominance over time
The USA has promised to give up power tomorrow
Hegemonies always last forever
No other country will ever grow
solution: The chapter suggests that US hegemony, though currently dominant, may not be PERMANENT. Reasons include: HISTORY shows that hegemonic powers eventually DECLINE (no dominance lasts forever); the RISE of NEW POWERS and centres of influence (such as CHINA, the EUROPEAN UNION, INDIA, and others) is gradually creating potential challengers and a more multipolar balance; the USA faces ECONOMIC CHALLENGES and the costs and OVEREXTENSION of maintaining global dominance (e.g., expensive wars); and the international BALANCE of power can SHIFT over time. These factors may erode US pre-eminence in the future. So US hegemony may not be permanent given historical patterns and rising powers. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The dominance of the US dollar in world trade and finance is an example of US __________.
options: Structural power (hegemony)
Soft power only
Military weakness
Cultural exports
solution: The dominance of the US DOLLAR as the world's principal reserve currency and the main currency for international trade and finance is a prime example of US STRUCTURAL POWER (hegemony). Because so much of the global economy's transactions, reserves, and pricing (e.g., of oil) are conducted in dollars, the USA gains enormous influence over, and benefits from, the structure of the global financial system (an advantage sometimes called an 'exorbitant privilege'). This system-shaping economic dominance is 'structural' rather than merely military (hard) or cultural (soft) power. So dollar dominance exemplifies US structural power. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The US invasion of Iraq in 2003 revealed both the strength and the limits of US hegemony. Reason (R): The USA could easily invade and topple the regime militarily, but it struggled to establish lasting stability and faced widespread international and domestic criticism. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the 2003 Iraq invasion revealed BOTH the STRENGTH and the LIMITS of US hegemony. And the reason is (R) that the USA could EASILY invade Iraq and TOPPLE Saddam Hussein's regime through overwhelming MILITARY force (demonstrating its strength/hard power) — but it then STRUGGLED to establish lasting STABILITY, order, and legitimacy in the aftermath (facing a prolonged insurgency and chaos), and it drew widespread INTERNATIONAL and DOMESTIC CRITICISM (for acting unilaterally on discredited grounds). This gap between easy military victory and the difficulty of achieving durable political success, amid criticism, precisely illustrates both the power and the limits of hegemony (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): Soft power is an important component of US hegemony. Reason (R): The global appeal of American culture, values, and lifestyle influences people's aspirations and preferences worldwide, extending US influence beyond military and economic means. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that SOFT POWER is an important component of US hegemony. And the reason is (R) that the global APPEAL of American CULTURE, VALUES, and LIFESTYLE (its films, music, brands, universities, and ideals) INFLUENCES people's aspirations and preferences around the world — drawing them toward American norms and shaping what they want — thereby EXTENDING US influence BEYOND purely military (hard) and economic (structural) means. This attractive, preference-shaping power is precisely what makes soft power a key element of US dominance (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The USA's ability to maintain a huge network of military bases around the world contributes to its hegemony by __________.
options: Giving it global reach — the ability to project military power quickly to almost any region
Reducing its influence
Isolating it from other countries
Weakening its military
solution: The USA maintains an extensive network of MILITARY BASES around the world (in many countries and regions). This vast base network contributes to its hegemony by giving it GLOBAL REACH — the ability to PROJECT military power quickly and effectively to almost ANY region of the world, to respond to crises, deter or coerce adversaries, protect allies and interests, and secure strategic locations and sea lanes. Such worldwide military presence is a key pillar of US hard-power dominance. So the base network gives the USA global military reach. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The chapter notes that even a hegemon like the USA cannot completely ignore __________.
options: World opinion, international norms and institutions, and the reactions of other states — since legitimacy, cooperation, and long-term interests still matter
Its own military
Its economy
Its allies' existence
solution: The chapter notes that even a dominant hegemon like the USA cannot COMPLETELY IGNORE certain factors: WORLD OPINION, international NORMS and INSTITUTIONS (like the UN and international law), and the REACTIONS of OTHER STATES (allies and rivals). This is because LEGITIMACY (being seen as acting rightfully) makes exercising power easier and cheaper; COOPERATION from others is needed for many goals (trade, security, tackling global problems); and the hegemon's own LONG-TERM interests are served by a stable, rule-governed order rather than by constant unilateralism that provokes resistance. So even the hegemon must reckon with world opinion, norms, institutions, and other states. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is a correct pairing of US hegemony 'type' with its example?
options: Hard power — US military dominance and invasions; Structural power — dominance of the dollar and global economic rules; Soft power — Hollywood, American brands, and universities
Hard power — Hollywood; Soft power — nuclear weapons; Structural power — pop music
Structural power — the US army; Soft power — the dollar; Hard power — American films
All three types mean the same thing
solution: The correct pairing of the three types of US hegemony with their examples is: HARD POWER — US MILITARY dominance and its ability to wage wars/invasions (e.g., Afghanistan, Iraq); STRUCTURAL power — the USA's shaping of the global ECONOMIC system, exemplified by the dominance of the DOLLAR and its influence over global economic rules and public goods; and SOFT power — the USA's CULTURAL influence, exemplified by HOLLYWOOD, American BRANDS and consumer culture, and its UNIVERSITIES/education. So option 1 gives the correct pairings. This is a useful summary for prelims.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'US Hegemony in World Politics' is that:
options: The USA is just one ordinary country among many with no special power

After the Cold War the United States emerged as the sole superpower, and its hegemony operates through hard power (unmatched military might, seen in the 'War on Terror' and the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq), structural power (shaping the global economy, e.g., the dominance of the dollar and provision of global public goods), and soft power (the worldwide appeal of American culture, values, and lifestyle); yet this hegemony is not unlimited — it is constrained by the USA's own separation of powers, its open society and free press, and international institutions and other states — and it may not be permanent as new powers rise; countries like India must decide how to respond (through strategies such as working with, balancing, or extracting benefits from the hegemon) while protecting their own interests and autonomy
The USSR dominates world politics today
US power is purely military with no other dimensions
solution: The chapter's overall message is that, after the end of the Cold War, the UNITED STATES emerged as the SOLE SUPERPOWER, and the world became characterised by US HEGEMONY. This hegemony operates in three key dimensions: (1) HARD POWER — the USA's overwhelming and unmatched MILITARY might and global reach, dramatically displayed in the response to 9/11 (the 'War on Terror') and the invasions of AFGHANISTAN (2001) and IRAQ (2003, undertaken largely unilaterally on discredited grounds); (2) STRUCTURAL power — the USA's role in shaping the STRUCTURES of the global economy and system (e.g., the dominance of the US DOLLAR and the provision of global 'public goods' like open sea lanes); and (3) SOFT power — the worldwide APPEAL and INFLUENCE of American CULTURE, VALUES, consumer lifestyle, entertainment, and universities. However, the chapter stresses that US hegemony is NOT UNLIMITED: it is CONSTRAINED by the USA's own internal institutional structure (separation of powers), by its OPEN society and FREE PRESS/public opinion, and by international INSTITUTIONS and other states/coalitions; and, like all hegemonies in history, it may NOT be PERMANENT, as new power centres (China, the EU, India, and others) rise. Finally, countries like INDIA must decide how to RESPOND to US hegemony — through strategies such as bandwagoning (working with and gaining from the hegemon), balancing (building coalitions and alternative centres of power), or a pragmatic mix — while safeguarding their own national interests and STRATEGIC AUTONOMY. So the overall message is option 2.

stem: The USA's military dominance is reflected in the fact that its defence spending is __________.
options: Far greater than that of any other country (indeed, more than the next several powers combined)
The smallest in the world
Equal to that of every other country
Zero
solution: The USA's military dominance (hard power) is reflected in its DEFENCE SPENDING, which is FAR GREATER than that of any other country — indeed, US military expenditure has been more than the combined spending of the next several highest-spending powers. This massive spending funds its unmatched arsenal, advanced technology, and worldwide network of bases and forces, underpinning its global military superiority. So US defence spending far exceeds that of any other country. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The First Gulf War (1991), in which a US-led coalition expelled Iraq from Kuwait, was significant because it __________.
options: Demonstrated the USA's military dominance in the new post-Cold-War era and its ability to lead a large international coalition (with UN backing)
Was a defeat for the USA
Was fought against the USSR
Had no international support
solution: The First Gulf War (1990–91) began when Iraq (under Saddam Hussein) invaded and annexed KUWAIT. A large US-LED international COALITION (with United Nations authorisation) launched 'Operation Desert Storm' and swiftly EXPELLED Iraq from Kuwait. This war was significant because it came right at the start of the post-Cold-War era and DEMONSTRATED the USA's overwhelming MILITARY DOMINANCE and its ability to organise and LEAD a broad international coalition (with UN backing and even some financial contributions from allies). It signalled the arrival of the US-dominated unipolar world. So the First Gulf War showcased US military dominance and coalition leadership. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The term 'hegemony' originally derives from the idea of __________.
options: Leadership or dominance of one over others (the pre-eminence or dominance of one state/group over the rest)
Equality among all
The absence of any leader
A type of economy
solution: The term 'HEGEMONY' derives from the idea of LEADERSHIP or DOMINANCE of one over others — the PRE-EMINENCE, dominance, or leadership of one state (or group) over the rest. In international politics, a 'hegemon' is a dominant power that leads and shapes the international system and over which no rival can prevail. Applied to the post-Cold-War USA, 'hegemony' captures its position of overwhelming, unrivalled dominance in world affairs. So hegemony means the dominance/leadership of one over others. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following best describes a limitation the USA faced in Afghanistan and Iraq despite its military superiority?
options: Winning the initial military battle was easy, but achieving lasting peace, stability, and political order (nation-building) proved extremely difficult and costly
The USA could not even win the initial battles
The USA faced no difficulties at all
The wars were fought without any soldiers
solution: A key limitation the USA faced in both Afghanistan and Iraq — despite its military superiority — was that WINNING the INITIAL military battle (toppling the Taliban and Saddam Hussein's regime, respectively) was relatively EASY, but ACHIEVING lasting PEACE, STABILITY, and functioning political ORDER afterwards ('nation-building') proved extremely DIFFICULT, prolonged, and COSTLY (in lives, money, and effort). Both countries slid into insurgency, violence, and instability that dragged on for years. This gap between military victory and durable political success revealed an important limit of hard power/hegemony. So the limitation was the difficulty of achieving lasting stability after easy military victory. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The concept of 'balance of power', as a way to constrain a hegemon, means __________.
options: Other states building up their own power or forming coalitions so that no single state can dominate them all
One state having all the power
Abolishing all states' power
The hegemon balancing its own budget
solution: The concept of 'BALANCE of POWER' as a way to constrain a hegemon means that OTHER STATES build up their OWN POWER (military, economic) and/or form COALITIONS/alliances with one another, so that COLLECTIVELY they can match or counterbalance the dominant power — ensuring that NO single state can DOMINATE them all. By preventing any one state from becoming overwhelmingly powerful and unchallenged, a balance of power can check and moderate a would-be hegemon. So balance of power means states building up or combining their power so no one state dominates. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The rise of which country is most often cited as a potential long-term challenge to US hegemony?
options: China (with its rapid economic and military growth)
Nepal
Bhutan
Fiji
solution: The rise of CHINA is most often cited as the leading potential long-term CHALLENGE to US hegemony. China's RAPID and sustained ECONOMIC GROWTH (becoming the world's second-largest economy), its expanding MILITARY power and technological advances, and its growing global influence have made it the most significant emerging rival to American dominance — a key factor in the possible shift from a unipolar toward a more multipolar world. So the rising challenger most cited is China. So option 1 is correct. (Other rising centres like the EU and India are also relevant, discussed in the next chapter.)

stem: The '911' / War on Terror period also raised concerns about __________, showing a tension within hegemony.
options: Human rights, civil liberties, and the treatment of prisoners/suspects (e.g., issues around detention and surveillance) versus security
The price of oil only
Sporting events
Space exploration
solution: The post-9/11 'War on Terror' period raised serious concerns about HUMAN RIGHTS and CIVIL LIBERTIES — showing a tension within the exercise of hegemony (and within democracies). Controversies arose over matters such as the DETENTION and TREATMENT of prisoners and terror suspects (e.g., detentions without trial, and allegations of harsh interrogation/torture), and expanded SURVEILLANCE — pursued in the name of SECURITY. These raised difficult questions about balancing security against rights and the rule of law, and drew criticism at home and abroad. So the War on Terror raised concerns about human rights and civil liberties versus security. So option 1 is correct.

stem: For India, being able to leverage its large pool of skilled professionals and its IT industry in relation to the USA is an example of India __________.
options: Taking advantage of the opportunities within the US-dominated global system to advance its own interests and growth
Militarily conquering the USA
Cutting off ties with the USA
Giving up its economy
solution: India's ability to leverage its large pool of SKILLED PROFESSIONALS and its strong IT INDUSTRY (e.g., Indian software companies, professionals working in and with the USA, and the technology partnership) in relation to the USA is an example of India TAKING ADVANTAGE of the OPPORTUNITIES available within the US-dominated global system to advance its OWN economic INTERESTS and GROWTH. Rather than merely resisting hegemony, India benefits from engagement — using globalisation and close economic/technological ties with the USA to boost its development. (This reflects the 'bandwagoning'/engagement strategy.) So it exemplifies India using the opportunities of the US-led system for its own advancement. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The USA can act unilaterally in world affairs. Reason (R): As the sole superpower with unmatched military and economic power, it faces no rival strong enough to force it to always act through international consensus. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the USA can (and sometimes does) act UNILATERALLY in world affairs (e.g., the 2003 Iraq invasion without clear UN authorisation). And the reason is (R) that, as the SOLE SUPERPOWER with UNMATCHED military and economic power, it faces NO RIVAL strong enough to FORCE it to always act through international consensus or to prevent it from acting alone when it chooses. Its overwhelming, unrivalled power is precisely what enables this unilateral capacity (A). So R correctly explains A. (Note, however, that other factors — legitimacy, cooperation, world opinion — still constrain it somewhat.)

stem: Assertion (A): US hegemony may decline over time. Reason (R): Rising powers, economic burdens, overextension in wars, and the historical pattern of hegemonic decline all suggest that no dominance lasts forever. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that US hegemony MAY DECLINE over time. And the reason is (R) that several factors point that way: the RISE of new POWERS (China, EU, India, etc.) creating potential rivals and a more multipolar balance; ECONOMIC BURDENS and challenges; the costs and OVEREXTENSION involved in fighting distant wars and policing the world; and the HISTORICAL PATTERN that hegemonies eventually DECLINE (no dominance has lasted forever). Together these reasons support the expectation that US dominance may erode (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The role of the USA in providing 'global public goods' (like keeping sea lanes open for trade) is significant because __________.
options: Such goods benefit many countries and help the global economy function, giving the USA a legitimising, system-sustaining role (part of its structural hegemony) even as it also serves US interests
It has no benefit to anyone
It only harms other countries
It is purely military conquest
solution: The USA's role in providing certain 'GLOBAL PUBLIC GOODS' — such as using its navy to keep the SEA LANES of communication OPEN and secure for international TRADE, or its early role in developing the internet — is significant because such goods BENEFIT MANY countries and help the GLOBAL ECONOMY function smoothly. By supplying these system-sustaining benefits, the USA gains a LEGITIMISING, ORDER-MAINTAINING role (a key aspect of its STRUCTURAL hegemony) — others accept its leadership partly because it provides useful public goods — even as this role also serves the USA's OWN interests (secure trade, a stable order favourable to it). So providing global public goods legitimises and sustains US structural hegemony while also serving US interests. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is the MOST accurate statement about the post-Cold-War international order?
options: It is US-dominated (unipolar/hegemonic) but not entirely without constraints or challenges, and it is evolving as other powers rise
It is perfectly bipolar
It is leaderless and chaotic with no dominant power
It is dominated by the United Nations alone
solution: The MOST accurate statement is that the post-Cold-War international order is US-DOMINATED (unipolar/hegemonic) — with the USA as the pre-eminent power in military, economic, structural, and soft-power terms — but NOT entirely without CONSTRAINTS or CHALLENGES (the USA is checked to some degree by its own institutions and society, by international norms and organisations, and by other states), and it is EVOLVING as OTHER POWERS (China, the EU, India, etc.) rise, potentially moving toward a more multipolar future. This balanced characterisation captures the reality better than the extremes of 'unchallenged empire' or 'leaderless chaos'. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The strategy of 'hiding' from the hegemon (as discussed in relation to dealing with US power) refers to __________.
options: A weaker state keeping a low profile and staying out of the hegemon's notice/way as much as possible to avoid being targeted or dominated
Physically becoming invisible
Directly confronting the hegemon
Joining the hegemon's military
solution: The strategy of 'HIDING' from the hegemon refers to a weaker state keeping a LOW PROFILE and staying OUT of the hegemon's NOTICE and way as far as possible — avoiding actions that might attract the dominant power's hostile attention, and thereby escaping being TARGETED, pressured, or dominated by it. Rather than either openly opposing the hegemon (balancing) or actively siding with it (bandwagoning), a 'hiding' state tries to remain inconspicuous and protect its autonomy by avoiding confrontation and visibility. So 'hiding' means keeping a low profile to stay out of the hegemon's way. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The dominance of American MNCs (multinational corporations) and brands worldwide reflects the __________ dimension(s) of US power.
options: Structural and soft power (economic reach through global corporations, and cultural influence through brands and consumer culture)
Only military power
Only the separation of powers
Weakness of the US economy
solution: The worldwide dominance of American MULTINATIONAL CORPORATIONS (MNCs) and BRANDS reflects the STRUCTURAL and SOFT dimensions of US power. It is STRUCTURAL power in that these giant corporations extend America's ECONOMIC reach and shape the structures of global production, finance, and technology; and it is SOFT power in that American BRANDS, products, and consumer CULTURE (fast food, technology, clothing, entertainment) spread American lifestyles, tastes, and aspirations across the globe, enhancing US cultural influence. So US MNCs and brands reflect structural and soft power. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The USA's response to 9/11 (the War on Terror) affected many countries, including those in India's neighbourhood, because __________.
options: Operations in Afghanistan and the wider region drew in neighbouring states (like Pakistan) and reshaped regional politics and security
It had no effect outside the USA
It only concerned Europe
It ended all conflicts in Asia
solution: The USA's response to 9/11 (the War on Terror) affected many countries, including those in INDIA's NEIGHBOURHOOD. The military operations in AFGHANISTAN and the broader campaign against terrorism DREW IN neighbouring states — most notably PAKISTAN, which became a frontline US partner (with major implications for its politics, its role regarding the Taliban and militants, and the flow of US aid and pressure) — and RESHAPED REGIONAL politics and security across South and Central Asia (affecting India's strategic environment, cross-border terrorism issues, and great-power involvement in the region). So the War on Terror reshaped regional politics in India's neighbourhood. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A key insight of the chapter is that hegemony operates not just through coercion but also through __________.
options: Consent and legitimacy — others accepting or going along with the hegemon's leadership because they see benefits or share its values (not only because they are forced)
Only brute force at all times
Random chance
The weather
solution: A key insight of the chapter is that hegemony operates NOT JUST through COERCION (force and threats) but ALSO through CONSENT and LEGITIMACY. That is, the hegemon's dominance is sustained partly because OTHER states and peoples ACCEPT or go along with its leadership — because they SEE BENEFITS in the order it provides (security, prosperity, public goods), or because they SHARE or are attracted to its VALUES and culture (soft power) — rather than solely because they are FORCED to. This element of consent and legitimacy (the hegemon being seen as a leader, not just a bully) is what distinguishes durable hegemony from mere domination by force. So hegemony works through consent and legitimacy, not only coercion. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The most sensible overall strategy for India in dealing with US hegemony, as suggested by the balanced view, is to __________.
options: Pragmatically combine engagement and cooperation with the USA (to gain economic and strategic benefits) with the preservation of its strategic autonomy and the pursuit of a more balanced, multipolar world
Wage war on the USA
Completely submit to US dictates
Cut off all relations with the USA
solution: The balanced view suggests that the most sensible overall strategy for India is a PRAGMATIC combination: to ENGAGE and COOPERATE with the USA (leveraging trade, investment, technology, and strategic ties to gain ECONOMIC and STRATEGIC BENEFITS for India's development and security), while at the same time PRESERVING its STRATEGIC AUTONOMY (an independent foreign policy, not becoming a subordinate) and working toward a more BALANCED, MULTIPOLAR world order (through ties with other powers, regional cooperation, and multilateral institutions). This avoids the extremes of outright submission or futile hostility. So India should pragmatically balance engagement with the USA and its own autonomy/multipolar goals. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The invasion of Iraq (2003) was carried out by a US-led grouping described as a __________.
options: 'Coalition of the willing' (a group of states willing to join the USA, outside the formal UN framework)
United Nations peacekeeping force
NATO-only operation authorised by the Security Council
Warsaw Pact mission
solution: The 2003 invasion of Iraq was carried out by a US-led grouping described as a 'COALITION of the WILLING' — a group of states (led by the USA, with Britain and some others) that were WILLING to join the operation, assembled OUTSIDE the formal authorisation of the UN Security Council. The phrase highlighted that the action lacked broad UN legitimacy and relied instead on those states prepared to support the USA. So the grouping was a 'coalition of the willing'. This is a prelims-relevant term.

stem: The Al-Qaeda leader held primarily responsible for the 9/11 attacks was __________.
options: Osama bin Laden
Saddam Hussein
Muammar Gaddafi
Fidel Castro
solution: Osama bin Laden was the leader of the AL-QAEDA network held primarily responsible for planning and directing the 9/11 attacks on the USA. The USA's pursuit of bin Laden and Al-Qaeda drove the invasion of Afghanistan (where they were sheltered by the Taliban) and the broader War on Terror; bin Laden was eventually killed in a US operation in Pakistan in 2011. (Saddam Hussein was the ruler of Iraq — a separate target of the 2003 invasion.) So the Al-Qaeda leader behind 9/11 was Osama bin Laden. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The term 'unipolar' (used for the post-Cold-War order under US hegemony) refers to a world with __________.
options: A single dominant power/pole
Two dominant powers
Many equal powers
No powers at all
solution: The term 'UNIPOLAR' refers to an international order with a SINGLE dominant power/pole — one state so pre-eminent that it stands above all others, with no rival or bloc able to balance it. The post-Cold-War world under US hegemony is described as unipolar because the USA was the sole superpower. (This contrasts with 'bipolar' — two poles, as in the Cold War — and 'multipolar' — many significant powers.) So unipolar means one dominant power. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is an example of how international public opinion and protests responded to the exercise of US hegemony?
options: Massive worldwide anti-war protests took place before and during the 2003 invasion of Iraq
The whole world unanimously supported every US action
No one ever criticised US policy
Protests only occurred inside the USSR
solution: A notable example of how international public opinion responded to US hegemony was the MASSIVE, WORLDWIDE ANTI-WAR PROTESTS that took place before and during the 2003 INVASION of IRAQ. Millions of people in cities around the globe (and within the USA and its allies) demonstrated AGAINST the war, which they saw as unjustified and illegitimate. Although these protests did not stop the invasion, they illustrated the limits on the hegemon's LEGITIMACY and the capacity of global public opinion to challenge and criticise its actions. So worldwide anti-Iraq-war protests are an example. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The chapter suggests that one of the most effective ways to check US hegemony in the long run may come from __________.
options: The emergence of regional organisations, economic groupings, and rising powers that create alternative centres of power (a more multipolar world)
A single heroic individual
Abolishing all governments
The USA voluntarily disbanding its economy
solution: The chapter suggests that, in the LONG RUN, one of the most effective ways to check US hegemony may come from the EMERGENCE of ALTERNATIVE CENTRES of POWER — the growth of REGIONAL ORGANISATIONS (like the EU and ASEAN), ECONOMIC groupings, and RISING POWERS (such as China and India) — which, by developing their own strength and cooperating with one another, can create a more MULTIPOLAR world in which US dominance is balanced and moderated. (This theme of alternative power centres is developed in the next chapter.) So the long-run check may come from the rise of alternative centres of power. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The USA's soft power can sometimes undermine the appeal of its rivals from within their own societies. Reason (R): The attraction of American culture, consumer goods, and lifestyle can influence the aspirations of people even in countries whose governments oppose the USA. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that US soft power can UNDERMINE rivals from WITHIN their own societies. And the reason is (R) that the ATTRACTION of American culture, consumer goods, entertainment, and lifestyle can shape the ASPIRATIONS and preferences of ordinary PEOPLE even in countries whose GOVERNMENTS oppose the USA — drawing them toward American ways and values despite official hostility. This internal cultural attraction, working on people's desires beneath the level of state policy, is precisely how soft power can quietly erode a rival's position from within (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The overall relationship between hegemony and international institutions (like the UN) is that __________.
options: The hegemon both uses institutions to legitimise and extend its influence and is, to a limited degree, constrained by them — the relationship is two-sided
Institutions have no relationship with the hegemon
Institutions completely control the hegemon
The hegemon has abolished all institutions
solution: The overall relationship between hegemony and international institutions (like the UN) is TWO-SIDED. On one hand, the hegemon USES institutions to LEGITIMISE and EXTEND its influence — securing endorsement for its actions (as in the First Gulf War), shaping the rules and agendas of global bodies, and clothing its power in the authority of international consensus. On the other hand, the hegemon is also, to a LIMITED degree, CONSTRAINED by these institutions and their norms — needing their approval for legitimacy, and facing criticism or obstruction when it flouts them (as over Iraq in 2003). So the relationship is two-sided: institutions both serve and somewhat constrain the hegemon. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In conclusion, US hegemony is best understood as __________.
options: A real but complex and potentially temporary dominance — powerful across military, structural, and cultural dimensions, yet subject to internal and external constraints and to change as the world evolves
An eternal, absolute, and unchallengeable empire
A myth with no basis
Purely a military phenomenon with no other aspects
solution: In conclusion, US hegemony is best understood as a REAL but COMPLEX and potentially TEMPORARY dominance. It is genuinely POWERFUL across multiple dimensions — MILITARY (hard power), STRUCTURAL (economic/system-shaping power), and CULTURAL (soft power) — making the USA the pre-eminent force in world politics. Yet it is NOT absolute or unchallengeable: it is SUBJECT to internal CONSTRAINTS (US institutions and society) and external ones (world opinion, international institutions, and other states), and it is liable to CHANGE as the world EVOLVES and new powers rise. So it is a powerful but constrained and changeable dominance, not an eternal empire. So option 1 is correct.
